What has actually been learned

The trigger filter keeps earning its keep. The trigger rate has been exactly 50% in both graded cohorts — half of every book never fills. In a falling tape that is protection, not a missed opportunity: the longs that failed to fill (JNJ, BMY, TGT, NVDA, MET, JPM, CVX, BIIB) fell afterwards, and not filling them is worth more than the trades that did fill.

First stop and first target both landed this week. COP triggered on 09/14 and stopped for a clean −1.00R — no gap, filled at the stop, exactly as modelled. PEP triggered 09/15 and reached Target 1 for +1.50R, the first realised target of the series. One of each is the minimum sample needed to confirm the exit machinery works in both directions, and it does.

Eight of ten triggered trades are still open, which means 4.15R is mark-to-market, not booked. It can still be given back. Treat the number as provisional.

Twenty plans is still not evidence of edge. Three weeks, one stop, one target, eight open positions, and a market that fell most of the way through. A short book will look brilliant in a tape like this whether or not the selection rules add anything. The honest claim is narrower: the rules execute as specified, the risk controls bind where they should, and the directional tilt has matched the tape. Ask again after a quarter, and especially after an up-week.

The logic, stated as rules

Every filter below is computed from split-adjusted daily OHLCV — nothing is discretionary, and nothing was chosen after seeing which names would pass. The rule set fuses four published frameworks: Weinstein's stage analysis for the regime a stock is in, Minervini's trend template for whether it is in a genuine Stage 2 advance, the Donchian / Turtle channel breakout for the trigger, and volatility contraction plus volume signature for whether the base is being accumulated or merely drifting.

Long — Stage 2 trend template (all seven must be true)

  1. Moving-average stack. Close > 50 SMA > 150 SMA > 200 SMA, and close above all three.
  2. Slope. 200 SMA higher than 21 sessions ago and 50 SMA higher than 10 sessions ago — the trend is being renewed, not decaying.
  3. Proximity to high. Within 25% of the 52-week high. Leadership does not hide in the bottom of its range.
  4. Distance from low. At least 25% above the 52-week low — filters out dead-cat bounces off a Stage 4 base.
  5. Relative strength. RS in the top 30% of the universe, where RS is the IBD-style weighted excess return over SPY: 40% × 3-month, 20% each × 6-, 9- and 12-month.
  6. Liquidity. 20-day average dollar volume ≥ $50M, so a 10–40 share-lot or a spread fills without slippage.
  7. Base structure. Range depth ≤ 18% measured over the shortest of the last 25, 40 or 60 sessions that qualifies.

Long — setup trigger (base rules plus these)

  • Proximity to pivot. Price within 7% of the base high — close enough that a buy stop is a trade, not a hope.
  • Not extended. No more than 14% above the 50 SMA. A stock already 3–5 ATR extended is a bad breakout buy regardless of how good the trend looks.
  • Volatility contraction or accumulation. Either ATR% today ≤ its level 20 sessions ago, or ATR% ≤ 0.85× its level 40 sessions ago (the VCP signature); or up-volume ÷ down-volume over 20 sessions ≥ 0.95.

Short — Stage 4 breakdown (all six must be true)

  1. Inverted stack. Close below both the 50 SMA and 200 SMA, and 50 SMA below 200 SMA.
  2. Slope. 200 SMA or 50 SMA declining — supply is in control on at least one timeframe.
  3. Proximity to low. No more than 25% above the 52-week low.
  4. Damage done. At least 18% below the 52-week high — this is a broken stock, not a pullback in an uptrend.
  5. Relative weakness. RS in the bottom 30% of the universe.
  6. Distribution. Up-volume ÷ down-volume over 20 sessions ≤ 1.05 — rallies are not being bought.

Trigger adds: price within 7% above the 25/40/60-session base low, and not more than 14% below the 50 SMA (an already-collapsed stock mean-reverts violently and is a poor short entry).

Entry, stop and target construction

  • Entry. Stop order at the structural pivot — the higher of the base high and the 20-day Donchian high for longs, the lower of the base low and the 20-day Donchian low for shorts — plus a 0.10 ATR buffer through the level. No anticipation, no limit orders inside the base.
  • Stop. The wider of the nearest structural level (10-day extreme, base extreme, or nearest clustered S/R zone) offset by 0.30 ATR, capped at 2.2 ATR from entry. The Turtle system's 2N stop, with structure allowed to tighten it but never to widen it past 2.2N.
  • Target 1. Entry ± 1.5R. Take a third to a half off; move the stop to breakeven.
  • Target 2. The measured move — base height projected from the pivot — or 2.8R, whichever is further.
  • Trail. After T1, trail on the 20-day Donchian extreme in the opposite direction (the Turtle System-2 exit).
  • Sizing. Shares = $500 ÷ (entry − stop), capped at 30% of account notional per position.

How the levels on each chart were derived

  • Swing highs / lows. Fractal pivots — a bar whose high is the strict maximum (or low the strict minimum) of the five bars either side of it. Marked ▼ and ▲ on the charts.
  • Support / resistance zones. Three-bar fractal pivots from the last 15 months, clustered where they fall within 0.6 ATR of each other. Each zone carries a touch count and the date it was last tested — a level touched four times is a different object from one touched once.
  • Volume profile. Six months of daily bars, 80 price bins, each bar's volume distributed uniformly across its high–low range. POC is the highest-volume bin; the value area is the 70% of volume around it; HVN are local maxima above the 75th percentile (shaded purple — price tends to stall and rotate there); LVN are local minima below the 25th percentile (grey dotted — price tends to move through them quickly).
  • Donchian channels. 20-day and 55-day extremes, excluding the current bar.

Sources

Minervini trend template criteria — Deepvue, TraderLion on stage analysis. Donchian breakout lengths, the N/ATR volatility unit, 2N stop and 20-day trailing exit — the original Turtle trading rules. Volume-profile HVN/LVN/POC methodology — AlgoVistra, FXOpen on fixed-range volume profile. Price data via Yahoo Finance; live quotes, option chains, Greeks and the earnings calendar via the connected brokerage MCP.

The second breadth rule has now fired. Two weeks ago this report wrote: "Below 40% breadth, stop taking new longs entirely and run the short book alone." Breadth closed Friday at 34.9% — through that line, not near it. This week's book follows the rule as written: six shorts, and no new longs. The two long candidates below are included as watch-only, with full levels, so they are ready if breadth recovers through 40% — but the report is not recommending them this week. The cumulative record backs the rule: the long book is -1.52R and the short book +5.67R.

What the leadership is telling you

The decline has broadened out of consumer. For two weeks the short list was consumer discretionary and staples retail — one theme, expressed many ways. This week it spans six sectors. Utilities arrived via CEG, down 38% as the AI-power-demand trade unwinds. Real estate arrived via CSGP, 67.6% off its high and the deepest drawdown in the universe. Industrials arrived via CPRT. Communication services arrived via NFLX. That is a materially different signal from three weeks ago: not a rotation between groups, but a decline that is running out of places to hide.

Energy broke. Last week's long-side leader is gone — COP stopped out at −1.00R and now scores 56.2 with up/down volume of 0.79. CVX and XOM still pass the template but neither is setup-ready. The one group that was working for the long side stopped working.

What is left on the long side is defensive health care (ABBV, BIIB, JNJ, GILD, DXCM) and a single megacap tech name. That is a narrower, lower-quality long list than either prior week, and it is arriving at exactly the moment breadth says not to buy it.

Why some high scorers were not given plans

Three filters were applied on top of the raw ranking. Sector concentration — health care produced seven of the 22 long passers (JNJ, BMY, BIIB, VRTX, AMGN, DXCM, MRK); taking the top two rather than the top four keeps a single FDA or drug-pricing headline from hitting four positions at once, which is why BIIB (77.5) and VRTX (76.1) were dropped despite outranking NVDA. The same logic removed HD on the short side, since LOW already carries the home-improvement trade. Setup-ready only — MRK, ILMN, ABNB and CRWD pass the trend template but fail a trigger condition, mostly base depth above 18%. Extension — LULU (91.2) and APP (75.5) score well as shorts but sit 15% and 18.6% below their 50-day averages; entering there invites a mean-reversion squeeze.

ABBV and AAPL are watch-only
Correction to last week's report. Two open positions — MCD and CVX — were missing from the 09-12 book entirely. MCD was excluded by the two-per-sector cap (it scored 97.0, third on the short list, but NKE and LOW took both consumer-discretionary slots) and CVX by the setup-ready filter. Both rules are meant to govern new entries; neither should ever remove a live position from the book, because the result is a position held with a stale stop and no guidance. Both now have full cards below, and the selection step has been changed so that every open position is carried forward automatically regardless of how it screens. Thanks to VK for catching it.

Read this before placing anything

Six positions are already live, not four: AAPL long, CVX long, and NKE, LOW, MCD and PEP's runner short. Together they carry $2,982.39 of risk. Two need a decision rather than a hold — MCD's stop tightens to 256.61, and CVX is the one position this report recommends reducing or exiting outright.

No new longs this week. Breadth at 34.9% is through the 40% line this report set two weeks ago, and the cumulative record shows the long book at -1.52R against the short book at +5.67R. ABBV and AAPL appear below with complete levels and charts so they are ready the moment breadth recovers through 40% — but the recommendation this week is not to initiate them. ABBV in particular is a genuinely good-looking setup arriving at a bad moment; that is worth saying plainly rather than dressing up as a buy.

Every open card shows an entry line, but for a position already on, that line is an add, not a new trade. What changed is the stop, rolled forward on the new data.

Three genuinely new shorts — CPRT, CEG and CSGP — across industrials, utilities and real estate.

  • You are already at the cap. Six positions are live against a 4–5 suggested limit. The first action this week is subtraction, not addition: exit CVX, and consider whether MCD and NKE both need to be on given they are the same trade twice.
  • Take the liquid ones first. NKE and LOW have real option markets; CEG and CSGP do not. If you are trading options rather than shares, that ordering matters more than the score ranking.
  • NKE and PEP both report inside the holding window — 10/01 and 10/08. Decide now whether you will be flat before those prints, because a short carried into an earnings gap is a different trade from the one modelled here.
  • Do not add to the four already open unless you are deliberately scaling and have the risk budget.
  • If breadth recovers above 40%, ABBV is the first long to take, and AAPL the second. CVX is not on that list — it has already failed once.
  • If VIX breaks 22 with SPY below its 50-day (759.73), cut gross exposure rather than adding shorts — that is the regime where short squeezes are most violent.

Execution notes

  • Monday 2026-09-21 is the next session — a normal week. If a stock gaps through its trigger by more than 0.5 ATR, stand aside rather than chasing; the risk:reward the plan was built on no longer exists.
  • The option expiry is 25 DTE, not the usual 35–45. The 35–45 band points at the 2026-10-30 weekly, but CPRT, CEG and CSGP have almost no weekly open interest. Oct-16 is the only expiry with a real two-sided market on these names. Shorter expiry means faster theta — size accordingly and do not hold to the last week.
  • ABBV has no usable call market. Both strikes nearest the trigger return no quote at all; only the far 280 call prints a market. Shares only.
  • AAPL again cannot be sized inside the budget as a spread — one contract risks $568 at the stop. Shares.
  • CEG, CSGP and CPRT have wide option spreads (26%, 22% and 18% on the long leg). Work limits into the middle or trade the shares; marketing into those quotes gives away most of the edge.
  • Confirm the breakout on volume. A trigger that fires on below-average volume is a lower-quality signal. The plan does not enforce this mechanically, but a breakout day below 1.2× the 50-day average volume deserves a half-size entry.
  • Options are for the trend, not the trigger. All ten structures are 38-DTE debit verticals expiring 2026-10-16. If a trade stops out in the first week, you lose roughly the delta-adjusted amount shown in each card, not the full debit — that is the basis contract counts were sized on. If you cannot honour the stop, trade shares instead.
  • Two names report INSIDE the holding window, not merely before expiry: NKE on 2026-10-01 (8 trading days out) and PEP on 2026-10-08 (13 days). A 3–15 day swing entered Monday is very likely still open on both dates. This is a harder constraint than in prior weeks — plan the exit around the print, not the option expiry.
  • Re-run the scan on any 2%+ index day. Base depths, Donchian levels and the pivot itself move; a plan built on Friday's close is stale after a large directional session.

What would invalidate this whole report

The risk has flipped sides. With breadth at 34.9% and a book that is now six-sevenths short, the dangerous scenario is no longer a further decline — it is a reversal. Readings this depressed are where violent counter-trend rallies start, and the most beaten-down names squeeze hardest. A breadth thrust back through 45%, or SPY reclaiming its highs on expanding participation, would hurt this book badly and fast. The specific tell to watch is the short candidates ceasing to make new lows while the index holds: NKE, LOW, MCD and PEP are all within 2% of 52-week lows, and if they stop breaking while SPY is flat, the trade is finished.

The other invalidation is unchanged: VIX above 22 with SPY below its 50-day (759.73, 0.3% below Friday's close). That is a regime where everything correlates to one and position sizing matters more than selection.
